name: Badlands
notes: Eroded clay and shale slopes mostly bare, with junipers in ravines, low sage and prickly pear on benches and short grasses in the flats; Dakota/Montana badlands with Bardenas Reales (Spain) and Patagonian analogues.

growth.juvenile_note: Hypogeal: the acorn stays in the soil and the seedling puts most of its energy into a taproot (1.4 m deep in the first year) while the shoot is small with a few wavy-lobed leaves. Sapling twigs often grow corky ridges. On prairie edges, fire-killed tops resprout from the root for decades ('grubs') before one stem escapes as a slender sapling.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (seed-bearing from ~35 yr, best 75-150; good crops every 2-3 yr; ~30% germinate within a month of seedfall; first-year roots 1.37 m; height growth 0.09-0.52 m/yr; lifespan 200-300 yr; to 52 m); USDA FEIS (remnants 300-400 yr, one ~440; shade-intolerant)

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics and FEIS Quercus macrocarpa (flowers Apr to mid-Jun; acorns ripen in one season and drop Aug-Nov; 0.9 g in Minnesota to 7.5 g and 5 cm in Texas, with a deep fringed cup covering a third or more; large crops in most years, every 2-3 yr); per-tree crop estimated

growth.juvenile_note: Cottony seed germinates within 24-48 h on wet, bare sandbars and mud flats; the seedling has two minute cotyledons and grows slowly for about 3 weeks, then very fast. Dense, even-aged thickets of slender single-stemmed whips form along river bars, with large triangular, coarsely toothed leaves on flattened stalks that flutter; saplings add 1.5-3.5 m a year on good sites.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 2 (P. deltoides: germination within 48 h; slow first 3 weeks then very rapid; seed from 5-10 yr, plains ~10 yr; 1.8-3.7 m/yr; very intolerant of shade; short-lived, 80-90 yr); USDA FEIS (eastern 100-200 yr, plains ~90 yr; 3-58 m tall).

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics vol. 2 (flowers Feb-Apr east, Apr-May plains, before leaves; male catkins 8-13 cm, female 15-30 cm; 3-4-valved capsules with 30-60 seeds ripen in 30-60 days; up to 48 million seeds per tree; wind pollinated); FEIS (capsules 0.8-1.5 cm). Colour is the red male catkins.

canopy.name: Ponderosa pine

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 6-12 cotyledons; in its first months it drives a taproot 50 cm deep while the shoot stays short, with single primary needles, then long needles in bundles of three. Saplings ('blackjacks') are narrow cones with dark grey-black bark and long, tufted, yellow-green needles; bark turns to orange puzzle-plates with age.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Oliver & Ryker): first cones at age 7, most seed at 60-160 yrs; taproots reach 50+ cm within months; dominants grow 0.24-0.46 m/yr up to age 60; intolerant of shade; commonly lives 300-600 years

canopy.source: western North America; 30–50 m. Vanilla-scented orange plates; open parkland forest. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings carry sharp, needle-like juvenile leaves and grow very slowly in the wild (about 30 cm in 8 years), forming a small, prickly, blue-grey cone that may flush purple in cold. Scale leaves take over at the sapling stage, and the young tree keeps a narrow, pyramidal, often multi-stemmed shape for decades before rounding out.
growth.source: USDA Silvics of North America vol. 1 (J. scopulorum: seedlings 30 cm in 8 yr, 4 m at 40 yr, 5 m at 80, ~9 m at 300; seed from ~age 10, heavy crops every 2-5 yr; cones ripen in 2 yr; 300 yr common, one reported 3,000; very intolerant but young relatively tolerant); USDA WPSM (120 d warm + 120 d cold stratification).

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (flowers mid-Apr to mid-Jun; cones 5-8 mm, bluish-purple with white bloom, ripen in 2 years mid-Sep to mid-Dec, persist to spring or up to 3 yr; prolific seeder); USDA WPSM (green with bloom before ripening). Set, crop and rot estimated.

shrub.name: Broom snakeweed

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds need no chilling and come up after spring or summer rain. The seedling is a single green stem with thread-narrow, resin-dotted leaves; it branches from the base in its first season and by the second is a small, rounded broom of many slender green stems, woody only at the base, topped in late summer with a flat spray of tiny yellow heads.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Gutierrezia sarothrae (subshrub 10-90 cm; short-lived, most plants under 10 yr, some to 20; seedlings flower in the first or second year; flowers Aug-Oct; populations cycle with wet years).

shrub.source: Gutierrezia sarothrae (Pursh) Britton & Rusby, broom snakeweed: rounded resinous subshrub 0.1-0.9 m of overgrazed and eroded plains, benches and badland slopes from the Dakotas and Montana to Mexico. Kew POWO; USDA FEIS; Flora of North America.

fruiting.source: USDA FEIS and Woody Plant Seed Manual Sarcobatus (monoecious, wind-pollinated; male flowers in small cone-like spikes at twig tips, female flowers single in leaf axils; tan winged utricles 4-5 mm, 1 cm across the wing, mature late Sep-Nov, a few hang until next summer)

Resprouts from stem buds after fire.

growth.juvenile_note: A single thread-thin, inrolled, grey-green leaf rises from the soil, then the seedling tillers slowly into a small tuft of wiry leaves; seedlings are slow and often lose out to established plants. Bunches enlarge by new crown tillers (each tiller lives about two seasons) into a fine, fountain-like tussock that sends up spikes of long, curly-awned 'needle and thread' seeds in early summer.
growth.source: NDSU autecology of needle and thread (tillers live two growing seasons, regeneration mainly by crown tillers, low seedling success, flowers late May-June); USDA NRCS Plant Guide (seed dormancy, slow establishment, flowers June, seed July); germination, growth and lifespan values estimated.

ground.name: Prairie sandreed

growth.juvenile_note: The seedling is a slow, narrow grass blade; it builds a deep root and from the second year sends out stout scaly rhizomes, so a plant becomes a loose colony of tall, stiff, leafy stems with long tapering leaves and, in late summer, a narrow tan panicle; dead stems stand through winter.
growth.source: USDA NRCS Plant Guide Calamovilfa longifolia (warm-season, strongly rhizomatous, 0.5-1.8 m, sandy soils of the northern plains, slow to establish); ages estimated.

ground.source: Calamovilfa longifolia (Hook.) Scribn., prairie sandreed: tall rhizomatous warm-season grass 0.5-1.8 m of sandy and sandy-clay soils in the northern Great Plains, including Badlands National Park. Kew POWO; USDA NRCS Plant Guide; Flora of North America.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are sparse, upright tufts of narrow, blue-green leaves with strongly ridged upper surfaces and claw-like auricles. Stands fill in slowly: rhizomes send up scattered, stiff, glaucous blue-green shoots forming an open sod, topped in summer by narrow, wheat-like spikes. Each shoot lives 2-3 years; the rhizome sod persists for decades.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Pascopyrum smithii (94% germination, mean ~12 days at 15/30 C, slow at constant 19-23 C; stands slow from seed, uniform sod in 2-3 years; flowers June-Aug, seed ripe Aug-Sep; tiller longevity 2-3 years in Saskatchewan); lifespan given per shoot (ramet)

ground.name: Wyoming rock-shield lichen

growth.juvenile_note: Begins as a small yellow-green lobed rosette on a pebble or on bare soil. The narrow, flat, shining lobes branch and spread outward; later the thallus often comes loose and lies free on the ground as a curled, crinkly yellow-green tuft 4-8 cm across, rolled about by the wind, black-brown beneath.
growth.source: Hale, monograph of Xanthoparmelia (thallus 4-8 cm, lobes 1-3 mm, often vagrant on soil); Eversman, Lichens of the Yellowstone ecosystem (vagrant on grassland soils); growth rates estimated.
